I'm Tushar, and I share a flat with Sudha. In March, during her final-year project, she seemed frazzled all the time: laptop, phone, music, food, all at once.
Then something changed. Every morning, before opening her laptop, she sat on the balcony for ten minutes with her eyes closed, just breathing. At first I thought she was sleeping.
She also started closing all her tabs except one while working. Phone in a drawer.
I asked her about it once. She said, "My mind was like a crowded bus. Now I'm trying to let people off."
I can't say how she feels inside. But she stopped snapping at me about the dishes, and she finished her project a week early.

qa.q: How long did Sudha sit on the balcony each morning?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What might Sudha have been feeling before the change?
qa.a: Sudha seemed frazzled and stressed, doing too many things at once.

qa.q: What habits could someone copy from Sudha to train attention?
qa.a: Short daily breathing practice, keeping only one tab open, and putting the phone away while working.

qa.q: How does Tushar see the change in Sudha?
qa.a: Tushar can't know her inner feelings but notices she is calmer and more productive.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young woman training attention through breath and single-tasking.

My first year living alone in Chennai, I thought freedom meant never cooking. I ate biscuits for breakfast and whatever for dinner. I stayed up until three watching shows.
By November I was always tired and caught every cold going round. My roommate Zeenat said, "You look like you're dissolving."

It took months to feel normal. But now I do it without thinking.

Pankaj, you're asking whether to let the AI write all your reports. Let me tell you about me and the calculator.
When I started as an accountant, calculators were new in our office. Some young people used them for everything and forgot how to check numbers in their heads.

It was 11:55 p.m. An email arrived for Mohit: "Your bank account will be blocked at midnight. Update KYC now." There was a link and the bank's logo.
Mohit panicked. Midnight was five minutes away. He clicked. The page asked for his card number and OTP.
He paused. His cousin Manjula, who worked in a bank, had told him: "Banks never ask for OTP."
He looked closely. The sender's address was a long string of random letters.
He closed the page, called the bank's official number from the back of his card, and they confirmed it was phishing. He forwarded it to the bank's report address and changed his password.
He texted Manjula: "Almost fell for it." She replied, "You didn't. That's what matters."

qa.q: What did the page ask for?
qa.a: His card number and OTP.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he clicked the link?
qa.a: Mohit felt panicked by the midnight deadline.

qa.q: What steps did Mohit take after noticing the warning signs?
qa.a: He closed the page, called the official bank number, reported the email and changed his password.

qa.q: How does Manjula see Mohit's near miss?
qa.a: Manjula focuses on the fact that he stopped in time, not on the mistake of clicking.

In the Pune office, Nitin kept hearing the word "data analysis" in meetings. He didn't understand the charts, and he felt left behind.
His colleague Sudha said, "There are free online courses. But don't just watch. Build something."
Nitin enrolled. Every evening, one hour. The first week, he watched videos and felt he'd learnt a lot. Then Sudha asked him to make one chart from the team's sales data. He couldn't.
So he changed: watch fifteen minutes, then practise on real data for forty-five. He made mistakes, searched for answers, asked Sudha on Fridays.
Three months later, he presented a chart in a team meeting. His manager asked who taught him. "Mostly myself," Nitin said. "And Sudha's Friday questions."

qa.q: How long did Nitin spend each evening at first?
qa.a: One hour.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he couldn't make the chart?
qa.a: Nitin felt frustrated, realising watching videos wasn't the same as learning.

qa.q: What change made Nitin's self-learning work?
qa.a: Spending less time watching and more time practising on real data, with regular questions to Sudha.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Nitin mentions her in the meeting?
qa.a: Sudha probably feels pleased and proud that her advice helped.

grounding: A young employee learns data analysis through a course plus practice on real projects.

"Tushar, you've started five online courses this year. How many did you finish?"
"…None. But I learnt bits."
Chaitanya laughed. "Same. I think we're collecting courses, not skills."
"So what do we do?"
"Pick one skill. For me, video editing. For you?"
"Web design."
"And one real project. I'll edit my cousin's wedding video. You?"
"My uncle's shop needs a website."
"Deadline?"
"End of the month."
"Mine too. Every Sunday, we show each other progress."
A month later, Tushar's uncle's site was live. It was simple. The contact form broke once. But it worked. Chaitanya's video made the family cry.

qa.q: How many online courses had Tushar started this year?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when admitting he'd finished none?
qa.a: Tushar felt embarrassed and a bit sheepish.

qa.q: What made their new learning plan work?
qa.a: Choosing one skill each, a real project with a deadline, and weekly check-ins with each other.

qa.q: How might Tushar's uncle feel when the website goes live?
qa.a: Tushar's uncle likely feels proud and grateful.

grounding: Two young adults switch from collecting courses to learning through real projects.

passage:
When I got my first office job, everyone used spreadsheets. I didn't know anything beyond typing numbers.
I was scared to ask. So on weekends, I watched short tutorials and practised with my own household budget. I made a mess. Formulas broke. But I kept a notebook of what worked.
My friend Simran, who worked in accounts, said, "Teach it to someone else. That's when you really learn." So I taught my younger cousin.
Six months later, my manager asked who could build a tracking sheet. I raised my hand.
I'm Sarita. No one taught me in a classroom. I learnt by doing, failing, noting and teaching.

qa.q: What did Sarita practise with on weekends?
qa.a: The household budget.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when too scared to ask?
qa.a: Sarita felt insecure and afraid of looking ignorant.

qa.q: What learning steps helped Sarita most?
qa.a: Practising on a real task, noting what worked and teaching a cousin.

qa.q: How might Simran feel hearing Sarita built the tracking sheet?
qa.a: Simran probably feels proud and happy that the tip helped.

grounding: A young adult recalls self-teaching spreadsheets through practice, notes and teaching others.

Career centre adviser's note.
Naveen, final year, came in today with a list of fourteen rejection emails. He said, "Maybe I'm just not good enough."
We went through them. Nine never gave feedback. Three said his technical round was strong but his communication weak. Two roles weren't a fit for his skills anyway.
I pointed out the pattern. He nodded slowly. "So it's not everything. It's one thing."
We booked three mock interviews focused on explaining his projects clearly. His friend Nikita, who got placed last month, offered to practise with him too.
He left looking tired, but less defeated. Follow-up in two weeks. — Mr Bose

qa.q: How many rejection emails did Naveen bring?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he said he might not be good enough?
qa.a: Naveen felt discouraged and doubtful after so many rejections.

qa.q: What did Mr Bose do that helped Naveen learn from rejection?
qa.a: He looked for patterns in the feedback, identified one specific area, and set up targeted practice.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel offering to practise with Naveen?
qa.a: Nikita probably feels supportive, remembering her own job search.

grounding: A career adviser helps a young man find patterns in rejections and keep going.

Dear Diary,
Rejection number twelve today. The email said, "We've decided to move forward with other candidates."
I cried in the bathroom. Then I called Manoj. He said, "Twelve is a lot. But remember, you only need one yes."
I made a spreadsheet: company, stage reached, feedback. I noticed I'm getting to final rounds more often now. In January I got rejected at the resume stage. Now I'm losing at the last step.
That's progress, even though it doesn't feel like it.
Tomorrow: ask the last company for feedback, update my portfolio, apply to three more.
— Vidya

qa.q: What number rejection did Vidya get today?
qa.a: Rejection number twelve.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when crying in the bathroom?
qa.a: Vidya felt hurt and discouraged by yet another rejection.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped turn rejection into learning?
qa.a: Vidya tracked applications and feedback and noticed getting further each time.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel supporting Vidya?
qa.a: Manoj likely feels caring and hopeful for Vidya's next try.

grounding: In a diary a young adult tracks rejections and notices progress.
